original_question: On which chromosome is the gene linked to the type I of the condition, which primarily affects the liver, and in which the body cannot effectively break down the amino acid tyrosine, located?

final_qi.question: On which chromosome is the gene linked to the type I of the condition, which primarily affects the liver, and in which the body cannot effectively break down the amino acid tyrosine, located?
final_qi.long_answer: Tyrosinemia type I is caused by mutations in the FAH gene (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase). Cytogenetic mapping places FAH at band q23-q24 of chromosome 15, establishing chromosome 15 as the locus linked to this hepatic form of the disorder in which tyrosine catabolism is impaired.

final_answer.long_answer: Tyrosinemia type I is caused by pathogenic variants in the FAH (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase) gene. This gene is situated on the long arm (q) of chromosome 15 at cytogenetic band 15q25.1. Defects in FAH impair the final step of tyrosine catabolism, leading to accumulation of toxic metabolites that chiefly damage the liver, producing the clinical picture of tyrosinemia type I.

1.question: Which gene is linked to type I of that condition?

final_answer.long_answer: Hereditary tyrosinemia type I is caused by mutations in the fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) gene. The FAH gene is mapped to chromosome 15 (cytogenetic location 15q25), so the defective gene responsible for type I tyrosinemia resides on chromosome 15.
